69211.etyen:
Inherited from Middle Norwegian vera (“to be”), from Old Norse vera, earlier vesa, from Proto-Germanic *wesaną (“to be”). The infinitive and past-tense stem continue Proto-Indo-European *h₂wes- (“to dwell; stay”). The present tense er, from Old Norse er, earlier es, belongs to the suppletive present-tense paradigm ultimately inherited from Proto-Indo-European *h₁es- (“to be”).
Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk vere, Danish være, Swedish vara, Icelandic vera, Faroese vera, Dutch wezen (“to be”), and English was and were. / Inherited from Old Norse viðra (“to blow; scent”), from Proto-Germanic *wedrōną (“to expose to the weather”), a derivative of Proto-Germanic *wedrą (“weather”), whose further origin is uncertain. Related to vær (“weather”).
Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk vêre, Danish vejre (“to scent”), Swedish vädra (“to air; scent”), Icelandic viðra (“to air; ventilate”), and German wettern (“to storm; rant”).

Egypt in Saint Ann Parish is historically recorded as one of the free villages established around Brown's Town after the abolition of slavery.

en.g: The twenty-seventh letter of the Norwegian Bokmål alphabet, written in the Latin script

1000283.etyen:
From the Latin ligature ⟨æ⟩, formed by joining ⟨a⟩ and ⟨e⟩. The Latin sequence ⟨ae⟩ originally represented a diphthong but later developed a monophthongal pronunciation, allowing the joined character to be associated with a single front vowel.
The character was adopted with the Latin alphabet into medieval Scandinavian writing and used to represent native front unrounded vowels. In Danish and Norwegian, ⟨Æ, æ⟩ became established as an independent letter rather than merely a typographical ligature. Swedish and German instead developed the corresponding letter ⟨Ä, ä⟩, originally formed with a sm

a male given name from Old Norse
x: Torbjørn kommer på besøk i morgen.
Torbjørn is coming to visit tomorrow.

1001307.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Þorbjǫrn. The Old Norse name consists of Þórr (“Thor”) + bjǫrn (“bear”), literally “Thor-bear”.
The first element Þórr is from Proto-Germanic *Þunraz (“Thor, god of thunder”), a personification of *þunraz (“thunder”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂- (“to thunder”). The second element bjǫrn is from Proto-Germanic *bernuz (“bear”); its deeper Indo-European origin is uncertain.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Torbjørn, Danish Torbjørn and Torben, Swedish Torbjörn, Icelandic Þorbjörn and Faroese Torbjørn (“male given names”).

en.g: a surname originating as a patronymic [in turn transferred from the given name, in turn from Latin, in turn from Ancient Greek], originally meaning “son of Aleksander”

1001563.etyen:
From Aleksander (“male given name”) + -sen (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””), originally a patronymic meaning “son of Aleksander”. The given name Aleksander is a Norwegian spelling of Alexander, representing Latin Alexander, from Ancient Greek Ἀλέξανδρος (Aléxandros).
Compare Danish Alexandersen and Swedish Alexandersson (“patronymic surname”).

en.g: to be well, be doing well; to be in a satisfactory state, especially with regard to one's health or general well-being

1001819.etyen:
A fixed phrase consisting of the imperative ha (“to have”), the pronoun det (“it”) and adverbial bra (“well”), literally “have it well”. As a farewell, the phrase is an imperative wish that the addressee continue to be well. The shortened farewell ha det (“goodbye, bye”) is an ellipsis of this expression or ha det godt (“goodbye, take care”).

en.g: Gudbrand Valley, Gudbrandsdalen (a valley and historical district Norway)
x: Gudbrandsdal med lange ermer, krøker seg rundt jotunbarmer, sterkt i størknede famntak støpt - Tore Ørjasæter
The Gudbrand Valley with long sleeves, curves around bosoms of Jotun, strongly cast in solid arms

1004123.etyen:
Most likely named after a powerful Norwegian tribal chief called Dale-Gudbrand, said to live in Hundorp in the Gudbrand Valley during the 1100s, with a status as a hersir (a local leader in early medieval Scandinavia), according to the saga Heimskringla written by Icelandic poet and historian Snorri Sturluson.
The male given name Gudbrand comes from Old Norse Guðbrandr, first part guð (“God, deity”), from Proto-Germanic *gudą (“god, deity”), from earlier *guþóm. Last part brandr (“brand, fire, sword”), from Proto-Germanic *brandaz (“fire, flash, flame, burning, sword”).

1004891.etyen: From kastanje (“chestnut”) + farget (“coloured”), literally “chestnut-coloured”. The first element kastanje (“chestnut”) was borrowed via German Kastanie (“chestnut”) from Italian castagna (“chestnut”), from Latin castanea (“chestnut tree; chestnut”), ultimately from Ancient Greek κᾰ́στᾰνᾰ (kắstănă, “sweet chestnut”). The second element farget (“coloured”) is based on farge (“colour”).

en.g: brouhaha, fuss, commotion, uproar; noisy excitement or disturbance
x: Det ble mye halløy rundt saken.
There was a lot of fuss surrounding the matter.
byen var taalmodig og overbærende med halløien deres av den grund, at paa havaristene tjente den brilliant
the town was patient and indulgent with their commotion, because it made excellent money from the shipwrecked men

1005147.etyen:
Borrowed from Danish halløj (“commotion, fuss”), a substantivization of the Danish interjection halløj (“hello, hey”). The interjection was apparently remodelled from hallo (“hello”) after words such as hej (“hi”) and ohøj (“ahoy”). The further origin of Danish hallo is uncertain.
Compare the parallel Swedish formation Swedish halloj (“hello, hey”) and the similarly formed Norwegian Bokmål Norwegian Bokmål halloi (“uproar, commotion; hello, hey”).
